title: A fabric called Plant Armor helps strawberries grow more
summary:
Researchers at North Carolina State University say a new fabric might help farmers grow more strawberries. It is called Plant Armor. In tunnel field tests, strawberry plants covered with Plant Armor produced yields as much as 3.56 times higher than uncovered plants. The researchers say it showed no harmful effects on plant health. They also say it may help reduce water use and the need for pesticides, which are chemicals used to kill pests.

Plant Armor is placed right over strawberry plants. It has a three-dimensional structure that makes a barrier to keep insects from reaching the plants. But the layered material still lets sunlight, rain and air pass through. Gabriel Olawuyi, a graduate research assistant and lead author of the paper, said, "To produce fruit, plants need sunlight." The team had expected the cover might block too much light, but the fabric did not reduce light.

The fabric also created a steady warming effect over three growing seasons. Olawuyi said that extra warmth helped covered plants reach the fruiting stage earlier. Because the fabric keeps insects from feeding on the plants, it could also reduce the amount of conventional pesticides needed.

The idea did not start with farming. It came from research on making military uniforms more resistant to mosquito bites and making body armor more comfortable for soldiers. Co-author R. Michael Roe said, "We couldn't have predicted that when we started." The paper was published in the journal Agriculture.
why_it_matters: Growing more fruit while using fewer pesticides could help farmers and the environment. The story also shows that research in one field, like clothing, can lead to surprising uses in another.
